title: Ivo and the Well
premise: August Underhill takes a teaching post at Hollow Fen Primary, a school where children vanish from the register one by one and no one will say why. The nightly sleep recordings meant to monitor the students begin capturing a second voice—patient, familiar, answering questions the children never asked aloud. August learns the school was built over an old wishing well that grants identity in exchange for memory: it is slowly replacing the town's children with versions of themselves that belong to it. When August discovers his own name appears in a ledger predating his birth, he realizes he was sent here as part of the count. In the end, August sacrifices his own recorded voice to jam the well's tally, spiriting the remaining families out ahead of the final reckoning—but the last recording captures a third voice, one that sounds exactly like him.
about_author: D. M. Montrose is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent nine years in isolated district schools before turning to horror full-time. Their work draws on folk traditions of wells, ledgers, and counting rhymes, and they insist all their books are read with the lights on.

chapters.title: The Register
chapters.summary: August arrives at Hollow Fen Primary to find twenty-two names on the roll but only nineteen children present, and the headmistress, Mrs. Vane, refuses to discuss the discrepancy. His POV establishes his habit of invisibility—counting doors, keeping lights on. The emotional beat is unease: the missing three are marked 'transferred' in handwriting that matches his own.

chapters.title: Nineteen Small Beds
chapters.summary: From the night matron Tilda's POV, we see the boarding wing where every child sleeps under observation. August reviews his first sleep recordings and hears nothing unusual—yet each child murmurs the same phrase at 3:11 a.m.: 'not yet, not me.' The beat is creeping dread beneath bureaucratic calm.

chapters.title: Doors Counted Twice
chapters.summary: August's POV. He begins his own private census of the building and finds a door on the lower corridor that appears on no floor plan, always locked, warm to the touch. A child named Wren tells him matter-of-factly that 'the well-teacher' counts them too. Beat: the hunter realizes he is also hunted.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Listening to Wren's sleep recording, August hears a second voice—low, unhurried, asking questions like 'do you remember your mother's face?' The child answers honestly, and each answer costs her something; by morning she misremembers her own middle name. Beat: horror becomes intimate and specific.

chapters.title: What Vane Knows
chapters.summary: Mrs. Vane's POV, the first break from August. She reveals the school sits atop a wishing well that has kept Hollow Fen prosperous for two centuries, paid in identities: the well doesn't take lives, it takes selves, leaving compliant shells. She believes this is stewardship, not evil. Beat: the antagonist's chilling sincerity.

chapters.title: Transferred
chapters.summary: August investigates the three 'transferred' children and finds their families gone, houses empty, neighbors unable to describe them. In the parish archive he finds a ledger listing every child ever given to the well—and his own name, dated forty years before his birth. Beat: identity itself becomes untrustworthy.

chapters.title: Wren's Question
chapters.summary: Wren, sharp and half-resistant, asks August directly whether he is real or already the well's. He cannot answer. They form a fragile alliance; she shows him how the children hide small true memories in counting rhymes so the voice can't collect them. Beat: defiant tenderness against erasure.

chapters.title: The Count Begins
chapters.summary: A new name vanishes overnight—registered as transferred before anyone reports it. Vane announces a 'full audit,' and staff begin recording children around the clock. August realizes the audit isn't safety; it's harvest inventory. Beat: the machinery of the horror accelerates.

chapters.title: Tilda's Tape
chapters.summary: Tilda secretly gives August a ten-year-old recording: the second voice once spoke to her, too, and she survived by giving it a false memory instead of a true one. But the price shows—she can't recall her sister at all. Beat: hope with a scar attached.

chapters.title: Inheritance
chapters.summary: August traces the ledger's oldest entries to the Underhill family, founders of the school, sworn 'keepers of the count.' He was not assigned here; he was returned. The well has been waiting for its heir to resume the tally. Beat: the theme of inheritance turns predatory.

chapters.title: Vane's Offer
chapters.summary: Vane offers August the headship: keep the count willingly, choose which children go, and spare the rest—including Wren—for another generation. It is power dressed as mercy, and part of him wants it. Beat: corruption knocks politely and is tempted.

chapters.title: The Locked Door Opens
chapters.summary: August opens the unmapped door and descends to the well shaft, where the walls are lined with names scratched by generations of hands. The second voice speaks to him directly, using his childhood nickname that no living person knows. Beat: confrontation with the source, and with himself.

chapters.title: Not Yet, Not Me
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The voice comes for her during the audit recordings, and she fights back with her rhyme-hoard of true memories. She holds—but loses her memory of August entirely, greeting him the next morning as a stranger. Beat: victory that devastates.

chapters.title: Half a Man
chapters.summary: August examines old recordings of himself sleeping and finds the second voice has been visiting him since his first night, patiently subtracting. He can no longer remember his mother's face or why he became a teacher. Beat: the protagonist's identity crisis made literal.

chapters.title: The Families Run
chapters.summary: August and Tilda quietly warn the parents still whole enough to listen. Some refuse—the well's prosperity is real—and one father reports them to Vane. Three families agree to flee before the final count. Beat: loyalty tested, community fractured.

chapters.title: Audit Night
chapters.summary: Vane locks down the school for the full count. Every child is recorded simultaneously; the second voice moves bed to bed like a toll collector. August sabotages the system, buying hours, while Vane watches him with something like pity. Beat: open warfare inside institutional order.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Choice
chapters.summary: Cornered in the ledger room, August understands the mechanism: the count requires a willing keeper's voice to authorize it. Vane pleads with him to accept the inheritance; the well, through the recordings, promises to give back everything he's lost. Beat: the climax of temptation—power offered at its fullest price.

chapters.title: Jamming the Tally
chapters.summary: Climax. August records himself surrendering false memories wholesale—a flood of invented confessions, wrong names, contradictory histories—until the well's count chokes on unverifiable selves. The shaft shudders; the locked door seals itself. Vane, betrayed by the failed audit, falls toward the well rather than live uncounted. Beat: sacrifice through self-corruption turned weapon.

chapters.title: Ahead of the Count
chapters.summary: August leads the surviving families out of Hollow Fen before dawn, Wren among them though she still doesn't know him. Tilda stays behind voluntarily—someone must keep the lights on, or the well will simply start again elsewhere. Beat: bittersweet exodus, duty as penance.

chapters.title: Empty Registers
chapters.summary: Weeks later, August teaches at a coastal school, keeping his rituals: lights on, doors counted. The children are ordinary, forgettable, gloriously unremarkable. He begins writing down every memory he fears losing, including ones about a girl who hid truths in rhymes. Beat: cautious healing, vigilance as love.

chapters.title: The Third Voice
chapters.summary: Reviewing a routine sleep recording of his new students, August hears a second voice ask its patient questions—and then a third voice answer. It is his own voice, calm and fluent, giving away true things. The well has learned to wear its keeper. Beat: dread rekindled at the personal level.

chapters.title: Ivo and the Well
chapters.summary: Final chapter, framed as the book you have just read: August's written account, addressed to Wren, ending mid-sentence as if the writer were interrupted. An appended transcript shows the third voice reading the manuscript aloud, correcting details, improving it. The last line asks the reader, gently, whether they remember their mother's face. Beat: the horror closes around us.
